statement: Sticks come in bundles of 10. Ana has 3 bundles and 14 loose sticks. Ben has 4 bundles and 2 loose sticks. Who has more sticks, and how many more?

choices.misconception: I counted each bundle as 1 stick, so Ana had 17 and Ben had 6.
I compared only the loose sticks, 14 and 2.
I wrote Ana's sticks as 34, forgetting that her 14 loose sticks make another bundle.
I compared only the bundles: Ben has 1 more bundle, which is 10 more sticks.

hints: Can Ana make another bundle from her loose sticks?
Turn both amounts into ordinary numbers before comparing. Ten loose sticks make one more bundle, so regroup first. Then compare the two totals.
Ana has 30 sticks in bundles and 14 loose, so 44. Ben has 40 in bundles and 2 loose, so 42.

solutions.reliable: Ana has $30 + 14 = 44$ sticks. Ben has $40 + 2 = 42$ sticks. So Ana has $44 - 42 = 2$ more. The idea to keep: when there are 10 or more ones, regroup them into a ten before comparing.
solutions.elegant: Ana's 14 loose sticks make 1 bundle and 4 loose, so she has 4 bundles and 4 loose. Ben has 4 bundles and 2 loose. The bundles match, and Ana has 2 more loose sticks.

whyOnTest: Regrouping 10 ones into a ten is the heart of place value, and comparing bundles alone points the wrong way.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
